What Is Artificial Intelligence?

AI is not magic , it is maths, data, and computing power working together to make machines seem smart.

Start Here

So what actually is AI?

Artificial Intelligence is when a computer learns to do things that normally need a human brain , like recognising faces, understanding language, or making decisions. It learns from examples, not rules someone typed in.

Think of teaching a child what a "cat" looks like by showing them thousands of photos. AI works the same way , millions of examples, patterns spotted, behaviour learned.

The Definition

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the ability of a computer or machine to do things that normally require human intelligence, like learning, problem-solving, understanding language, and recognising patterns.

🐶
Think of it like training a dogYou show a dog what "sit" means over and over. AI learns the same way, from lots of examples, until it gets good at a task.
🎵
Like a music recommendationWhen Spotify suggests a song you love, that is AI noticing your patterns and predicting what you will enjoy next.
📷
Like face unlock on your phoneYour phone's camera learned what your face looks like and recognises it every time. That is AI at work.

AI combines data, algorithms and computing power to simulate intelligent behaviour.

AI In Everyday Life

AI is already all around you , you probably use it dozens of times every day without realising it.

Language

Chatbots, translation tools, voice assistants like Siri, and AI writing tools all use natural language processing to understand and generate human language.

NLP

Vision

Face ID, Google Photos, self-driving cars, and medical imaging all use computer vision to interpret the visual world in real time.

Computer Vision
🎯

Recommendations

Netflix, Spotify, YouTube, and TikTok all use AI to predict what you want to watch, listen to, or read next based on your behaviour.

A · The Vault

The faithful one. It keeps the photograph’s own luminance — a near-black warm ground, everything below mid-grey — and solves the readability problem at the other end, with warm cream type at 15.7:1. Parchment appears only in small pieces: a label, a stamp, a pull quote. Nothing you have to read for a minute sits on paper. One brass hairline and a wax seal are the entire ornament budget. This is the closest to the reference and the safest to build, because the site is already dark and only the hue changes.

B · The Archive

The literal one. Reading happens on paper, the way it does in the photograph — but the paper is brightened well past the reference, because the reference’s own paper cannot carry text. That is the honest cost of this direction and it is worth naming: at the photograph’s value the page is unreadable, and at a readable value it is lighter than the photograph ever gets. What you buy for it is the thing the image is actually about — documents, edges, deckle, the sense of handling something.

C · The Celestial Atlas

The one that does not throw anything away. The site already has a hand-built sky; this re-tints it from aqua to brass and sepia, and it stops being science fiction and becomes an eighteenth century star chart — which is exactly this palette, and exactly this paper. The globe and the pocket watch in your reference are from the same drawer as an orrery. It resolves the argument between “space site” and “antique” instead of picking a side, and it is the only one of the four that keeps the identity you have already built.

D · The Correspondence

The structural one. Instead of a texture, the photograph’s objects become the information system: a chapter is a letter, its number is a postmark, finishing one presses a wax seal, the planner is a ledger, a saved note is a card in a drawer. The look follows from that rather than being applied on top. It is the most distinctive of the four and the most work, because it changes what things ARE and not only what they look like.
